title: Reimagining Security for the Agentic Workforce

segments.text: >> ANNOUNCER: Please welcome President and
Chief Product Officer, Cisco, Jeetu Patel.
>> JEETU PATEL: How is everyone doing?
That is great; that is great.
Vasu is one of my dearest friends,
so it is great to follow her.
This is my fifth RSA; I'm delighted to be here for the
fifth RSA conference.
And this one is different though.
We are living in probably one of the most interesting times,
because it is the most exciting and simultaneously
the most disorienting times in human history.
And it all started three years ago when ChatGPT was launched.
And essentially what you had over here was a seminal moment
where it felt like magic, but it also was a very compressed
amount of time, within which all of a sudden it just started
feeling very normal.
It was actually the fastest amount of time from feeling
like magic to compressed to feeling like this was
just normal occurrence.
We are now entering into one of these other seminal moments
and the ChatGPT moment that happened for chatbots.
We have another ChatGPT moment, which is the OpenClaw
moment that happened again exactly three years later in
November for Agents.
And we are now squarely getting into the second
phase of AI, which is moving from these intelligent chatbots
that answered questions for us that felt like magic to now
Agents that conduct tasks and jobs for us
almost fully autonomously.
Now, the question you might ask is,
what is so different about Agents?
Well, they plan, they act entirely autonomously at times,
and the most important thing, what actually defines
an Agent is they have access to tools and systems that you use.
So we shouldn't think of these Agents as tools.
We should think of these Agents more like digital
co-workers that are going to be augmented to our teams
and to the tune of thousands within a company.
And you will be able to make sure that you
delegate tasks to them.
But the ability to, in a trusted form, delegate a task
versus just delegating a task, not being trusted,
is going to be the difference between being a market leader
versus being bankrupt.
And so there is a tremendous level of complexity that is
going to be associated with this.
Now, here is the catch with these digital co-workers.
You can't really go check their resumes.
You can't make reference calls to make sure that these Agents
are working well.
You can't do any background checks.
And so as you start to think about this, there is one more
thing that is that they follow instructions very literally,
and they operate without any fear of consequence.
I mean, what are you going to do, fire an Agent?
Right?
And so what you are starting to see is there is
a tremendous amount of complexity, because if you
give agency to someone to go operate completely in
an autonomous way, but they have no fear of consequence,
those things can get to be pretty scary.
Now, there is one more catch, is you have to give them access
to all your systems so that they can work on your behalf.
And these Agents are going to proliferate at a scale
proportion that is unlike anything we have seen before.
We are going to have trillions of these Agents.
Just think about it.
There is 8 billion people in the world.
For every person, you will have between 100 to 1,000 Agents,
maybe 10,000 Agents.
And so there is going to be a tremendous amount
of compounding effect.
And if you start to think about it, there is 150 million
developers on GitHub today.
Very soon, you will actually have three billion builders that
are starting to build and direct these Agents.
If you are a human being, you are going to be
a manager of Agents.
So, as we start to think about this, the risks that are
associated with managing these Agents and delegating work in
a trusted way compound at an exponential rate.
And the reason for that is because with chatbots,
the biggest risk was you had to worry about it giving you
the wrong answer.
With an Agent, you have to worry about it taking
the wrong action.
More importantly, with an Agent, you have to worry about
it not only just taking the wrong action, but taking an
action that is irreversible, which then has a meaningful
set of consequences.
Let me give you a very simple scenario just to make it real.
And so let's say that Jane wants to just plan a team
offsite in Napa.
So the first thing she does is she makes a request to an
Agent that says, "You know, go ahead and plan a team
offsite for me, but just make sure you handle everything."
And so the Agent gets right to work, and it starts
going out and planning.
And so it is going to do a bunch of planning.
It is going to start searching for venues.
It is going to start making sure that it is checking calendars.
It is looking at identifying hotels, so on and so forth.
And it is going to start connecting to these different
systems to make sure that these things are happening.
Now, it starts taking a bunch of actions next.
It says, all right, I have gone out and done the planning.
I got to take some action.
So it is going to start doing some actions,
but some of these actions might be out of bounds.
So it might say, I'm going to go ahead and book hotels on
a corporate card, but I'm not going to take
approval from anyone.
I'm just going to go ahead and book them.
I'm going to start sending invites to 80 people,
but two of those people happen to be ex-employees
that now work for a competitor.
Now I'm going to start looking at what the dietary
restrictions of people are, but I'm going to publish
those dietary restrictions so that everyone now has
those people's dietary restrictions at home addresses.
And then I'm going to grant access to an internal Slack
channel to the caterers who now not only have your
nut allergies, but they are also going to have
your product roadmap.
And so these are some of the things that are not completely
out of the ordinary.
These can completely happen with Agents.
And so the next thing, the next step, the next phase of
this entire cycle is what I call the oops phase.
Because the oops phase is when you start thinking about
sensitive HR data that got exposed.
You start thinking about a former employee who used to be
a competitor that now actually has gotten access
to some sensitive data.
The caterer has access to your roadmap, and so on and so forth.
Most importantly, the credit card got charged for $40,000.
So clearly, it doesn't take Jane that long to figure out
that something is wrong.
So what does it do?
It actually calls out the Agent, says, "Hey, this seems
like another disaster."
And the Agent's really polite, says, "I'm really sorry, note it
for the next time, but you're out $40,000."
And essentially, what we have done is created a condition
where the reality is that the apology is not a guardrail.
So what do we do in this scenario?
And what do we do as a security community because
to be honest, this entire equation that I gave
you actually sucks.
So what do we need to do?
We need to fundamentally reimagine security for the
Agentic workforce, completely rethink it.
And so what does that look like?
And there is three areas that this community must
focus on, I think.
The first one is that we need to make sure that we protect
these Agents from the world.
Whenever there is a world trying to go out and make
attacks on these Agents, we have to make sure that
we protect them.
Number two is we have got to make sure that we protect the
world from Agents that might go rogue.
And number three, we have got to make sure that we can
detect and respond at machine scale and speed, because no
longer can human scale and speed suffice when these Agents
are actually going out and working 7 by 24.
So let's talk about each one of these innovations that we have,
because this is a really interesting time where the
gravity of the body of work that all of you do is
more important now than ever before.
And so let's assume that you are going to have tens of
thousands of Agents within your organization, and we have
to keep them safe and secure.
Now, the way that it worked in the chatbot era is you only
had to worry about a user communicating with a model
and the interaction between a user and a model.
So what we had done was we had focused on safety and security.
Last year when I was here, I talked about this whole notion
of safety and security.
Safety being, what do we need to do to make sure that the
model doesn't misbehave?
If there is hallucination or if there is toxicity or
self-harm behavior that is starting to get exuded from
these models, we need to make sure that we can intercept it.
We can validate those models so we can intercept it.
On the security side, we need to make sure that if there is
an external attack that is happening on any of
these models, things like a prompt injection attack,
like Vasu talked about, things like jailbreaking,
those are things that we need to make sure that we can
also prevent against.
But with Agents, this gets far more complicated because now you
as a user aren't just connecting to a model,
you are connecting to an Agent.
That Agent might connect to a bunch of local Agents or
third-party Agents who are then going to use multiple
methods to access a multitude of tools and resources on your
behalf so that they can get the work done.
All of these tend to become meaningful exposure points.
As an industry, for decades, we focused on security to
protect humans, but we only have months to replicate what
we have done.
And by the way, what we have done for humans is
not even perfect.
We only have months now to go out and replicate that
success for Agents.
We might not even have months.
And so what we have to do is really start thinking about an
end-to-end way that these Agents get protected.
So when you start thinking about the multidimensional way
that you need to think about an Agent, there is a multitude
of different areas that you have to worry about from an
Agent deployment standpoint.
For example, if you think about using a model,
you need to make sure that you really think about, are we aware
of model vulnerabilities?
For the memory that you are going to have for that Agent,
is there evidence that there is no memory tampering?
If you have skills that are going to be directing the
Agent in some way or form, is that skill going to do
something reckless that you don't know about?
If you have tools and access to those tools, are the MCP
servers hiding malicious instructions that you need to
make sure that you intercept?
Now, you have to enrich these Agents with context.
Has poison data been injected for enriching that context?
And lastly, if you have a sandbox where you are going
to operate these Agents from, can the Agent escape
that runtime boundary?
These are all the kinds of things that you need to
be thinking about.
And so what we have been doing at Cisco is we have been
building tools to address this Agent safety and security
across all of these areas.
And so over the course of the past few months, we have had a
multitude of these tools that we have completely open
sourced because I think what is really important is making
sure that we work together as a community and provide tools
and knowledge to each other.
Because the true enemy over here is the adversary because
the adversary has access to the same Agents that they are
directing in a way that we don't want it to be directed.
And so we have this open source community where all of
these different tools, from a skill scanner to a AI bill of
materials to an MCP scanner, all of these tools
are available on GitHub.
In fact, the QR code is over there if you folks want to go
out and check out those tools.
These are completely free.
They are open source.
They are available for the community to use.
But that is not what we are stopping.
We are also launching a security framework that
activates these tools anytime that you deploy an
Agent, completely automatically.
And I'm delighted to announce today that we
are introducing DefenseClaw.
DefenseClaw is a security framework
for OpenClaw deployments.
That means if you are using OpenClaw and you want to make
sure that you are safe and secure with OpenClaw,
DefenseClaw will help you do that.
And by the way, this also is completely open-sourced.
And let me just give you some details on how this works.
How many over here went to the GTC conference last week or
watched Jensen's keynote?
Anyone?
There is a complete Venn diagram, no intersection.
So let me actually see if I can walk you through what was
announced last week.
NVIDIA announced something called OpenShell.
OpenShell is a secure container that an OpenClaw
Agent can run inside.
And so what we have done is we have taken DefenseClaw and we
have used hooks so that all those services that I talked
about can now automatically be instantiated when you have an
Agent running an OpenShell.
And so every single time an Agent executes with an
OpenShell, you are going to automatically activate these
open-source services so that it can actually go out and
scan the skills and make sure that it is checking
for vulnerabilities and scan the MCP servers.
And we won't stop there.
Expect us to continue to keep innovating and making sure that
we can actually double down, triple down, quadruple down
in the open-source community because we have to
make sure that these Agents are delegated work in
a trusted manner.
Because like I said earlier, the difference between
delegation and trusted delegation is the difference
between bankruptcy and market leadership.
So folks, that is protecting Agents from the world.
Second, let's talk about what we need to do to protect the
world from Agents.
Now, we have talked a lot about this notion of humans
in the loop.
And we always talk about the fact that at some point in time,
the human has to verify what the Agent is doing.
But the reality is that Agents are starting to get into
every single loop.
They are going to be accessing systems that take action.
They are going to be potentially doing things
that you never intended them to do.
And that is, by the way, a risky combination.
So for years, we have talked about this notion of zero trust
to provide what we call least privileged access to humans,
which means only give it permissions to a human to
do things that you want it to do.
And so the whole notion of this least privileged access
with zero trust was making sure that we activate that
with humans having access control, which means that the
human has to prove their identity and once they have
proven their identity, you are going to make sure that you
can trust the user.
With Agents, we are going to need to do much more than just
to access control.
With Agents, we are going to need to make sure that we move
our mindset from access control to action control,
which is going to need to verify behavior and provide
control to the Agent when the Agent's starting to go awry.
And so what is going to be needed to make this happen?
Three things.
First, we are going to need to make sure that we know every
Agent that is in your environment.
Second, we have to make sure that we can
authorize every action.
And third, we have to make sure that we can adapt to risk
in real time.
So let's dig into details in each one of these things.
For knowing every Agent, what we need to make sure that we do
is discover all Agents that you might have
within your environment.
You need to build an Agent directory of Agent identities.
And then you need to make sure that you can assign humans and
human owners some degree of accountability for every Agent
so that every Agent, some human is accountable for that
Agent and their behavior.
Then you need policies for what these Agents can and can't do.
And the way that you are going to enforce these policies,
you are going to authorize every single action.
So first, what are we going to do?
If you think about Agentic identity and access management
that sits in between an Agent workforce and the tools and
systems you are going to give it access to, it is going to
need to do three things.
First, you have to give it just-in-time permissions.
Basically saying, only when the Agent needs it, you give it
permissions right away.
Number two, you have to give it just enough permission.
It is this notion of least privileged access.
Don't over-permission the Agent because that is when
things can go sideways.
And number three, give it just for long enough so that it can
get the job done and then you revoke the permission right as
soon as the job is done.
Second, we can't do this everywhere that Agents live
because you can't trust the endpoint anymore.
The only thing you can trust is where they connect and that
is the network.
So from there, you also need to be able to dynamically
adapt to the risk in real-time.
So what does that look like?
Well, the way that the dynamic adaptation of risk looks like is
you have Agents, and those Agents are going to have
threat context, and they are going to have behavior context.
And you have to make sure that you actually enrich yourself
with a good understanding of what is happening for
both threat context and behavior context.
For example, an Agent trying to connect to a compromised
MCP server, that is threat context.
An Agent who has been given the right to delete an email and
starts to automatically delete 10,000 emails,
that is behavior context.
That is alarming that you might need to intercept.
And so we have to make sure that we actually have this
context so that we can stop bad things from happening.
So that is protecting the world from Agents going rogue.
Third, let's talk about detecting and responding at
machine speed and scale.
And when you think about detecting and responding at
machine speed and scale, think about Agents
being fundamentally relentless.
They work 7 by 24.
They don't need any quality of life.
They don't have a family to go to.
They are just working all the time.
And these adversaries that we have actually have access
to these Agents just like we do.
And so the compounding effect of the amount of attacks that we
are going to see are going to be very, very different.
So detection and response gets much, much harder in
this Agentic world.
And so if we were only limited to responding at human scale,
we would be on the cusp of an epic catastrophe.
Why is that?
Because right now, the primary kind of limiter for us is human
capacity when we start looking at this.
If you look at most of the vulnerabilities, 80% of the
vulnerabilities don't get patched because most of us
don't have the ability to fulfill the capacity to be
able to patch those vulnerabilities.
So you prioritize vulnerabilities and you just
ignore 80% of them.
All of us live that life.
So it is imposs --
What if, though, we could actually say every signal and
every alert that came through your system, we would be able
to make sure that we could investigate every signal
and every alert.
We believe this is actually within reach.
And the way it is within reach is through an Agentic SOC.
Because what you will be able to do is operate data at
ludicrous scale so that you can correlate data on
a constant basis.
And that is what an Agent would do in an Agentic SOC.
You would then make sure that these Agents are responding to
threats at machine speed, giving us a level of capacity
of scale that we have never before imagined.
And lastly, you can think about the reinforcement learning
that these Agents will have, where you can
incorporate data and the outcomes and the learnings have
become this continuous loop.
So the Agent keeps getting better and better and better.
It might start as a teenager, or it has become
a senior analyst very, very quickly.
And so you are going to need to hear much more about this
as the year goes on.
Make sure you catch the Splunk keynote later tomorrow so that
you can hear about that as well.
But to wrap up, here is what I want to say.
We have covered ground in three areas.
Number one, we have to make sure that these Agents don't
get manipulated by the world and they get protected.
Number two, we need to make sure that when Agents
start going rogue, we know exactly when to intercept.
And number three, we have to make sure that if something
has gone wrong at machine scale, not only do we know
how to detect, but we can respond and remediate
as quickly as possible.
Now, the way I think about this, let me leave you with
this one last thought, which is organizations that win won't
just deploy Agents.
They will make sure that those Agents are trustworthy.
And this is going to be probably the biggest
bottleneck of our time, is can we ensure that
Agents have delegated authority with trust?
So together, what we should do is make sure that
as a community, we come together.
All of us should be investing in open source.
All of us should be contributing in open source.
And let's unlock the full potential of AI by ensuring
that when we deploy AI, that AI is trusted AI.
Because this is not just good for your organization.
It is not just good for your country.
It is good for humanity.
It is good for the world.
Thank you all.
